sections.heading: 1. The verb ἐστιν ("is") and predicate nominative
sections.content: The most common pattern in this chapter is X ἐστιν Y — "X is Y." The verb ἐστιν (3rd singular present of εἰμί) links the subject to a noun or adjective in the same case (the nominative).

sections.heading: 2. The article ὁ ("the") — masculine
sections.content: Every noun in Part A is masculine, taking ὁ in the nominative singular and τόν in the accusative singular. The noun itself ends in -ος (nominative) and -ον (accusative).

examples.greek: ὁ γεωργός, ὁ οἶκος, ὁ ἀγρός

sections.heading: 3. Adjective agreement
sections.content: Adjectives match their noun in gender, number, and case. As predicates (linked by "is") they have no article; as attributives (modifying directly) they sit inside the article-noun frame.

sections.heading: 4. Present active indicative — 3rd singular
sections.content: Most verbs end in -ει for "he/she/it [does it]." Contracted verbs in -έω contract ε + ει → ει (e.g. φιλέ-ει → φιλεῖ).

sections.heading: 5. Present active indicative — 1st singular
sections.content: In the farmer's monologue, verbs shift to 1st person, ending in -ω. For "to be" we use εἰμί. The pronoun ἐγώ ("I") is added only for emphasis.

sections.heading: 6. Particles & connectives: μέν…δέ, οὖν, γάρ, καί
sections.content: These shape the rhythm of Greek prose: μέν…δέ sets up contrast ("on the one hand…on the other"), οὖν = "therefore," γάρ = "for, because" (always 2nd in its clause), καί = "and / also."

examples.greek: γεωργὸς μέν εἰμι. ἐγὼ δὲ ἔχω τὸν οἶκον

examples.note: for he is a strong man

sections.heading: 7. The dative case — "in/at" (location)
sections.content: New in Part B is the dative singular of masculine 2nd-declension nouns: ending -ῳ with article τῷ. With the preposition ἐν ("in") it expresses location. Without a preposition it marks the indirect object.

sections.heading: 8. The irregular adjective μέγας ("great")
sections.content: μέγας uses two stems: μεγα- in the masculine nominative singular, and μεγαλ- elsewhere (with -ν added for the accusative).
